posts.author: Jim McPherson
posts.content_md:
After getting back from a business trip, I hooked up my laser diode to try the new Photopolymer I got from Sergio. I set up an interferometer to make sure that the diode had warmed up suffeciently to start making holograms. But in my usual setup, I got no fringes at all.... nothing. I then moved the mirrors to within 1 cm of each other and all of a sudden I have very stable fringes. About a month ago when I last turned the laser on I had at least 1 foot of coherence length. This can be backed up by JohnFP who was witness to that. I've been running the laser at about 1/2-2/3's recommend power, and it is still very bright and putting out the same amount of energy, so it's not a "DED". Any ideas what I have done or what could be causing this in a laser diode?

-Jim

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md:
I suspect your diode has failed due to static electricity. One zap can blow off a facet, and then the resonator is toast. Usually this also results in reduced output as well.

I've had this happen several times to small diodes, even when the driver circuitry was attached. I have a drawer full of dead ones.

That's one reason why I switched to Henes. Heck, If a Hene doesn't start right away, I scrape up some static electrity and give 'em a 1/4 inch zap! -starts em every time!

posts.content_md: Jim, contact me, bring it over and let's play.

posts.author: Jim McPherson
posts.content_md:
Well after further review, when different path lengths are present, the fringes still appear but they are very small. After warm up they are extremely stable, not moving at all during a 1 min. time period. I widened the beam fairly large and could see small fringes. When moving the path lengths equal I can ge larger fringes, even one very large fringe. What does small and large fringes mean? Will this affect holography with the diode?

-Jim

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: The size of the fringes relates to the geometry of the interferometer. Try to align the two beams so that they are perfectly in line and you get a bullseye pattern for the most accurate results.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
> **Colin:** Try to align the two beams so that they are perfectly in line and you get a bullseye pattern for the most accurate results

Yes, and the largest fringes. Although ususally when I get the bulls eye in my set up I only see a fringe or two. 

If your fringes are running up and down move the right to left tilt of one of the mirror a very little bit. If the fringes get smaller then go the other way with the same adjustment. You should see them get bigger. At some point, like tweaking a spatial filter they will probably change to diagonal or across, where you would need to move the top to bottom mirror adjustment.

Play and you will see.
